title_en: As China continues to invest in AI, will its economic imbalances worsen?
content_en:
Louis Kuijs at S&P Global Ratings warns AI could deepen China’s economic imbalances which already see weak domestic demand unable to absorb output.
China may be set for greater economic imbalances if structural reforms do not happen in lockstep with AI advancement, a veteran sinologist says. Photo: EPA
Layering artificial intelligence onto China’s existing economic model without broader structural reforms could deepen the country’s economic imbalances, as businesses and capital owners stand to benefit more than workers and households, a veteran China watcher has cautioned.
“When productivity goes up, it may go up in a way that mainly benefits capital and doesn’t benefit labour,” said Louis Kuijs, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at S&P Global Ratings.
“If this is laid on top of the existing economic process in China, it will add to existing pressures.”
In an interview with the South China Morning Post last week, Kuijs, a former senior economist at the World Bank’s Beijing office, said the effects might be palpable in China, where the existing growth model channels a relatively small share of national income to workers and households.
“These issues about the lack of rebalancing may become more pronounced if AI adoption accelerates without adjustments in the economic policy setting,” he said.
China has made AI a central part of its drive to upgrade the economy and develop new growth accelerators, with Beijing issuing a series of national initiatives to promote the technology’s adoption across industries.
The country’s total AI-related spending was projected to reach about US$220 billion this year, according to a report released earlier this month by a research team affiliated with the China Finance 40 Forum.
An employee works on a smart technology-powered production in China’s eastern Jiangxi province on November 16. Photo: Xinhua
Yet the increase in AI-related capital expenditure across Chinese companies was expected to contribute less than 0.4 percentage points to gross domestic product growth, the report said.
Kuijs noted that without broader changes to China’s growth model, the benefits of AI-driven productivity gains could continue to accrue disproportionately to businesses and capital owners, rather than households – potentially further constraining household purchasing power, which is already weak.
That could leave China with another wave of overcapacity, this time in AI-related industries, if companies add capacity without a corresponding increase in domestic demand to absorb their output. Exports could again become an outlet for the surplus, he said.
Addressing the imbalance would require structural reforms, including improving access to health, education and social security and a clearer separation between the state and business, Kuijs said. Such changes, however, would take time to implement.
The reliance on exports to sustain growth was already evident in S&P Global Ratings’ latest economic projections, led by Kuijs and released on Monday. The agency raised its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5 per cent, from 4.3 per cent in its September projection, citing an AI-driven technology export boom.
But the credit rating agency projected domestic demand would remain weak through 2027. Strong exports were helping Beijing meet its growth target this year, allowing it to keep stimulus at a minimum, while S&P forecast some slowdown in economic growth next year.
[embedded media]
Kuijs said Chinese policymakers generally focus on broader indicators of economic performance, underpinned by strong exports and growth in the technology sector, making them less inclined to introduce further stimulus as long as the overall economy continued to perform well.
The persistence of these economic imbalances had raised concerns that China was moving closer to what economists call “Japanification”, according to Kuijs, referring to a prolonged period of weak growth and low inflation, similar to what occurred in Japan after its asset-price bubble burst in the early 1990s.
Decades ago, Kuijs said, economists would have firmly rejected the idea that China could follow a similar path. Now, he added, the question might have more relevance.
He noted, however, that China’s economic circumstances differed from Japan’s in the 1990s, particularly as the world’s second-largest economy still had considerable room for development.
“I think there’s still a lot of catch-up potential in China compared with where Japan was in 1990, so it’s a bit easier for China to still grow. If you have a bit more underlying growth, many things are much easier than without it,” he said.
By Alice Li

title_en: Could potential US tariffs put the US-China trade truce at risk?
content_en:
Any new duties would be unlikely to derail the agreement provided they remain capped at 20 per cent, according to analysts.
The US Capitol in Washington, US. Photo: Reuters
The United States could be paving the way for fresh tariffs on imports from 16 economies, including China and the EU, as it prepares to release the findings of a months-long investigation into excess industrial capacity.
Higher tariffs could be announced as early as this week, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the plans.
We examine the potential duties, the investigation behind them and what they could mean for Washington’s fragile trade truce with Beijing.
What is the investigation about?
The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) investigation under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act examines whether foreign government practices contribute to excess industrial capacity in ways that harm US commerce.
The probe covers 16 economies: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India.
Launched in March, the investigation forms part of the Trump administration’s efforts to rebuild its global tariff agenda after the US Supreme Court struck down its broad “Liberation Day” duties in February. The probe joined a separate Section 301 investigation into forced labour practices in 60 economies.
Any new tariffs are expected to be added to those announced in July from the forced labour probe, which imposed levies of 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent on goods from the targeted economies.
How would new US tariffs add to existing duties on China?
The US imposed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chinese imports under the forced labour investigation. Beijing has previously said Washington agreed during bilateral talks to cap any replacement tariffs on China at 20 per cent.
The two sides have successfully maintained a fragile trade truce, extended last month to run until January 10, though Washington tightened restrictions on advanced chip exports last week amid scrutiny of the administration’s failure to curb China’s access to advanced Nvidia chips through data centres in third countries.
China’s commerce ministry has voiced “strong dissatisfaction” with Washington’s new chip restrictions, though Beijing has so far held off on broad retaliation. On Tuesday, the ministry extended a waiver on export restrictions of critical minerals to the US by two months, including shipments of gallium, germanium and antimony, as part of a broader cooling of tensions between the world’s two largest economies.
Could new tariffs derail bilateral ties?
Xu Tianchen, a senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, expects any new Section 301 tariffs against China to be “capped firmly within 7.5 per cent”.
[embedded media]
“Otherwise, Trump will immediately lose China’s trust for breaking one of the underpinnings of the truce,” Xu said.
Beijing might not welcome the new tariffs, but the combined duties would be unlikely to provoke retaliation so long as they remained within the 20 per cent cap, he added.
President Xi Jinping is also expected to meet Trump at the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, which would mark their fourth meeting this year following talks in Shenzhen last week. “The two sides definitely want to keep their ties on track” ahead of the meeting, especially as the January expiry for the trade truce draws closer, Xu noted.
Hui Shan, Goldman Sachs chief China economist, said the number of times the two leaders had met in 2026 had made the year “highly unusual”.
“It is unlikely that there will be such frequent engagement next year,” Shan added, warning that economic uncertainties in the bilateral relationship could increase.
In a Wednesday note, ING senior economist Inga Fechner also wrote that the Democratic Party could try to dismantle Trump’s tariff regime when it takes control of Congress in January. But the president retaining executive power would make that difficult, Fechner added.
On Wednesday, China’s foreign ministry said tariffs were not in the interest of either Beijing or Washington. “The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manoeuvring,” spokesman Guo Jiakun said.
“Both China and the US should work together to implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and safeguard the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations,” Guo added.
By Xinyi Wu

title_en: US says Latin America is too dangerous – unless you are seeking asylum
content_en:
The State Department country reports are prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94 per cent.
A US Border Patrol vehicle pulls tires to clear a road along the US-Mexico border near Somerton, Arizona, on October 18. Photo: AFP
In its travel advisories, the US State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras’ Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.
But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report.
The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94 per cent during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that do not stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.
They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.
Police officers patrol near the site of a massacre in Trujillo, Honduras, on May 21. Photo: AFP
The reports had been “reverse-engineered”, said Elliot Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analysed the documents for the college’s Migration and Asylum Lab.
“They’re trying to hit the most frequent kinds of [asylum] cases that come up and provide counter-evidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.
The State Department did not respond to a request for comment on the reports. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.
‘Not legitimate’
Cutting back on asylum has been a centrepiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the US as “not legitimate asylum seekers”.
Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.
“Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status,” he said in a 2018 White House appearance.
Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.
But he had a point about poverty.
Migrants traveling north in a caravan toward the United States gather next to vehicles belonging to Mexico’s National Migration Institute after turning themselves in on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters
Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.
Even during President Joe Biden’s years, most asylum claims were rejected. But denials have jumped from roughly 72 per cent at the end of that Democratic administration to 94 per cent in June under Trump, according to the data research non-profit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.
Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.
The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organising mass hearings, authorising military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.
Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, “membership in a particular social group”.
They also have to show that their government cannot or will not protect them and that they cannot move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.
Downplaying dangers
The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries. They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that “the availability of services” can vary across each country.
Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.
The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government approach to rights abuses “is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself”, and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.
“In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power,” it says.
For Honduras’ Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates “compare favourably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States”, the report says.
Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

content_display:
The State Department country reports are prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94 per cent.
A US Border Patrol vehicle pulls tires to clear a road along the US-Mexico border near Somerton, Arizona, on October 18. Photo: AFP
In its travel advisories, the US State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras’ Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.
But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report.
The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94 per cent during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that do not stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.
They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

Cutting back on asylum has been a centrepiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the US as “not legitimate asylum seekers”.

title_en: China calls on Netherlands to help safeguard industrial and supply chains
content_en:
Appeal to visiting Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen comes amid drive to improve ties following last year’s row over chipmaker Nexperia.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen pictured with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing. Photo: EPA
China has called on the Netherlands to help safeguard supply chain stability and stabilise Beijing’s relations with the European Union, during Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen’s visit to Beijing.
The visit follows that of Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis earlier this week, making the pair the first top European diplomats to visit China following the historic three-way summit between Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, where they pledged to reduce nuclear risks and bolster global energy security.
Chinese Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang told Berendsen on Wednesday that the two countries should “make joint efforts to safeguard the stability and smooth flow of industrial and supply chains”.
In a separate meeting, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Beijing hoped the Netherlands would provide a “fair, transparent and predictable” business environment for Chinese enterprises.
“China attaches great importance to the Netherlands’ role as a gateway in China-Europe cooperation, and hopes the Dutch side will play a constructive role in the sound and steady development of China-Europe relations,” Wang said.
Berendsen stressed that the Netherlands was willing to strengthen high-level exchanges with Beijing, deepen cooperation across various fields and “properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation”, according to the Chinese foreign ministry.
It was Berendsen’s first trip to China since taking office in February. Before travelling to Beijing, he visited Dutch tech companies and a Chinese robotics start-up in the southern tech hub Shenzhen.
He served as a member of the European Parliament for over six years before becoming foreign minister. In Brussels, he built his profile as one of the sharpest critics of Chinese state-linked influence over critical infrastructure, supply chains and digital networks.
Ding Chun, director of the Centre for European Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said Berendsen’s trip meant economic, trade and technological cooperation had been given a “relatively high priority”.
Despite Berendsen’s previously hawkish stance towards Beijing, the current Dutch administration was a minority coalition, and the visit signalled that a fragile cabinet was seeking to stem economic losses, he added.
Ties between the two countries came under strain during last year’s stand-off over Dutch chipmaker Nexperia, but relations have since eased through renewed high-level diplomacy under the new government.
Earlier this month, the two sides held talks on export controls, agreeing to maintain close communications and work together to “keep semiconductor and other supply chains stable and unobstructed”.
The Dutch government has also rejected the bipartisan US Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (Match) Act, a proposal that aims to curb advanced chipmaking equipment exports to China and has gained momentum following espionage allegations involving Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
The Dutch foreign ministry said “extraterritorial measures” in the bill were “unacceptable” between partners, according to Politico.
“The Netherlands needs to safeguard the commercial interests of its own companies while still aligning with the US security framework – it has constantly been trying to strike a balance,” Ding Chun said.
The Dutch diplomat’s trip is also aimed at preventing the Nexperia row from further eroding the Netherlands’ credibility as an investment destination, as well as securing a stable and predictable regulatory environment for companies such as ASML, he added.
The dispute over Nexperia – a Dutch semiconductor manufacturer acquired by Chinese firm Wingtech Technology in 2019 – has escalated sharply over the past year.
Following Dutch government intervention and court rulings that suspended Wingtech’s management control, a Dutch court this month empowered court-appointed administrators to seek outside investors while barring the Chinese parent firm from interfering. Wingtech has vowed to challenge the decision.
Fudan University’s Ding noted that the Netherlands was seeking to strip Chinese investors of control, whereas Chinese firms viewed the move as a forced expropriation of legitimate investments.
Such a fundamental clash could not easily be resolved in a diplomatic visit aimed at managing differences, avoiding direct confrontation and preventing decoupling, he said.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen (right) visits robotics company LimX Dynamics in Shenzhen. Photo: Handout
On Monday, in talks with Cassis, Wang said that China-Switzerland cooperation had proved that “protectionism is no panacea and converging interests are by no means a security risk”.
The talks marked the fifth round of foreign ministers’ strategic dialogue between China and Switzerland.
The Chinese diplomat reiterated his call for the Swiss side to help facilitate “a smooth resolution” of economic and trade differences between Beijing and Brussels.
“China and Europe should break free from the so-called trade imbalance narrative trap, properly manage differences through dialogue and consultation, and achieve mutual benefit and win-win results by expanding the pie of cooperation,” Wang said.
China has long viewed Switzerland, which is not a member of the European Union, as a trailblazer among European nations in building ties with Beijing.
The contrast between China’s relations with Switzerland and the EU has sharpened in recent months, as Beijing and Brussels struggle to manage mounting trade tensions amid the looming threat of a trade war.
In a meeting with Swiss President Guy Parmelin in Beijing last month, Xi highlighted the two countries’ free-trade agreement as the “brightest calling card” of their relationship amid rising currents of unilateralism and protectionism.
Xi also underscored Switzerland’s “important exemplary role” in economic relations between China and Europe, urging him to help foster the steady growth and balance of trade.
During the Swiss president’s visit, the two countries upgraded their free-trade agreement, which took effect in 2014 as the first such pact between China and a continental European nation.
In recent months, Beijing and Bern have also maintained communication on international flashpoints, including the conflict in Iran.
By Fan Chen, Carol Yang

title_en: Bangladesh garment workers win 36% minimum wage rise after protests
content_en:
The hike is the smallest percentage increase since the sector’s first minimum wage was set in 1986.
Bangladeshi police charge at garment workers with batons during a demonstration demanding higher wages in Gazipur, on the outskirts of Dhaka, on Wednesday. Photo: AP
Bangladesh’s garment workers won a 36 per cent minimum wage increase on Wednesday, officials said, after weeks of sometimes violent protests that caused hundreds of millions of dollars in business losses.
The South Asian nation, the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, has seen widespread demonstrations since October by workers demanding higher pay.
The garment industry, which clothes millions of consumers across Europe and North America, is Bangladesh’s economic lifeline, accounting for four-fifths of export earnings and employing more than four million people.
Following lengthy negotiations with factory owners, workers’ representatives urged employees to return to factories.
“Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either,” Babul Akhter, the workers’ representative on a wage board set up to resolve the crisis, told reporters.
“Previously, workers used to get a wage revision every five years, but this time they are getting a revised wage after three years.”
Garment workers leave a factory amid protests in Gazipur, Bangladesh, on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters
The hike was the smallest percentage increase since the sector’s first minimum wage was set in 1986. Wages were raised by 56 per cent in 2023, 51 per cent in 2018 and 77 per cent in 2013.
“These negotiations result in poverty wages time and time again,” said Anne Bienias, the Clean Clothes Campaign’s living-wage coordinator, adding that the new pay rate remained well below a living-wage level.
On Wednesday, several hundred protesters set up barricades in the industrial zone of Gazipur, on the outskirts of the capital Dhaka, some hurling rocks, before police dispersed them using tear gas and stun grenades.
Police official Amzad Hossain said officers were “trying to keep things under control”. Protests later eased, although several factories remained closed.
“Do you think we should be happy with the raise?” asked Al Amin, a worker in Gazipur. “The increased salary still does not match the rising prices of commodities … But I guess most workers want to return to work.”
Kamrul Hasan, senior union official from the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, said that while the increase fell short of demands, they accepted the offer.
“Workers should also consider the situation of medium and small factories – they would not be able to pay much more and would eventually shut down,” he said. “The unrest will gradually recede.”
Mahdi Amin, the prime minister’s adviser on labour, welcomed the pay rise and urged calm. “Let us not be influenced by any kind of propaganda, provocation or misinformation,” he said, the state-news agency BSS reported.
Rising costs
Workers initially demanded a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$240), up from 12,500 taka. They say their pay had failed to keep pace with the rising cost of food, housing, transport and healthcare.
Judge Syed Azad Subhani, the chairman of the government-appointed garment industry wage board, said the “majority supported a minimum wage of 17,000 taka”, after a vote early on Wednesday.
The wage hike will take effect in January.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday that protests had cost the industry an estimated US$428 million in losses, while orders worth US$254 million had shifted to other countries. The disruption came ahead of the busy Christmas season.
The garment industry, which supplies major international brands including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss, earns around US$38 billion a year.
Bangladesh supplies more than 150 countries with ready-made garments, according to the BGMEA, which represents around 4,000 factories. The United States is its biggest individual market, while the European Union is its largest trading bloc.
When Bangladesh won independence from Pakistan in 1971, it was among the world’s poorest countries, with its economy devastated by war.
The expansion of garment production helped transform the nation of around 170 million people from a predominantly agricultural economy into a major global manufacturing hub.
Bangladesh’s central bank calls the garment sector the “country’s export engine”. But its success has been built on a vast, relatively low-paid workforce, with long-standing disputes over wages, working conditions and labour rights.
Garment workers head to their respective factories in Gazipur on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters
An industry leader warned that while the higher wage would improve workers’ incomes, it could further erode Bangladesh’s competitiveness.
“At US$138, we now pay more than West Bengal in India and about the same as Vietnam, Indonesia and Pakistan. Low cost was our main edge, and it’s gone,” said Mohiuddin ‌Rubel, additional managing director of Denim Expert, which supplies ‌to brands including H&M.
“The capability gap, not the wage gap, now decides orders. So the government must help us build capability through cheap long-term credit for man-made fibre, automation and skills, and faster port and customs clearance, so we can compete with our rivals.”
He also urged international brands to share part of the higher labour costs.
“Buyers are our partners and the biggest stakeholders, so sharing the higher wage cost is their responsibility too,” he said.
“We have already cut prices by 6.54 per cent in Europe so far this year and still lost volume, and small factories cannot absorb the new wage bill alone. Brands should ring-fence the wage cost in their prices.”

title_en: Doctor accused of indecent examination deviated from usual practice, hearing told
content_en:
Three doctors testify as witnesses during inquiry at medical watchdog in case related to Dr Alvin Chan’s examination of patient’s genitals.
Dr Alvin Chan is charged with five counts of professional misconduct at the medical watchdog inquiry. Photo: Lo Hoi-ying
A renowned Hong Kong paediatrician facing allegations of indecently examining a male patient’s genitals without consent and making inappropriate remarks deviated from usual practice, expert witnesses have told an inquiry at the medical watchdog.
Three doctors testifying as medical practice witnesses on Wednesday told the Medical Council inquiry panel that Dr Alvin Chan Yee-shing’s examination of the patient’s genitals at Hong Kong Baptist Hospital was unrelated to his symptoms of dizziness, nausea and diarrhoea.
Chan is charged with five counts of professional misconduct: improperly and indecently examining a patient’s genitals on two occasions in April 2021; examining a patient’s genitals without just cause or consent; making inappropriate comments on the patient’s penis; and inappropriately writing his clinical treatment record using uncommon abbreviations in January 2022.
The patient, identified only as X to protect his privacy, accused Chan of removing his underpants without consent and stroking his thighs with his bare hands, saying he needed to examine his lymph nodes, which resulted in X getting an erection.
X alleged that Chan said he spotted lesions on his penis and needed to check for genital warts, forcefully pulling back his foreskin. Chan also allegedly used his forearm to touch his penis more than four times.
No chaperone was present during the incident, X added.
The case at the Medical Council has been adjourned until January 10 next year. Photo: Karma Lo
Chan then allegedly conducted another similar genital examination the following day.
Family doctor Gene Tsoi Wai-wang said that if patients accidentally got an erection during a medical examination, doctors should cover their genitals and let them rest for five minutes “as a matter of courtesy”.
Tsoi also said it was “prudent” that when doctors conducted intimate examinations of genitals, explicit consent be obtained and that patients had the right to refuse.
Nurses should also be called in as chaperones, which would be explained to the patient.

title_en: As Taiwan’s local elections loom, voters want an end to ‘constant confrontation’
content_en:
In New Taipei City, KMT and DPP supporters share some common ground, but relations across the strait remain a divisive issue.
A KMT rally in New Taipei City on Sunday drew a huge crowd of supporters, who responded in unison to chants from mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan. Photo: Handout
Campaign ads are everywhere on the streets of New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous municipality, as local elections loom across the island.
The vote will be a key test of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s political strength, but also the unity of the opposition parties. Officials ranging from mayors and county commissioners to councillors and village chiefs will be elected in 22 cities and counties across Taiwan on Saturday.
The most politically significant contests are playing out in New Taipei City and the nearby capital Taipei. The stakes are high, and the results could have big implications for Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te and the leader of the main opposition Kuomintang, Cheng Li-wun.
In New Taipei City – home to more than 4 million people – supporters at KMT and DPP campaign events share a common desire for stability in their lives. But they have very different views on how cross-strait relations and the status quo should be handled.
While the KMT has governed the area since 2005, support for the DPP and the KMT is relatively evenly divided in the lead-up to the polls.
Supporters in blue caps attend the KMT event in New Taipei City on Sunday. Photo: Holly Chik
At a KMT rally at a park on Sunday afternoon, an energetic crowd sat shoulder to shoulder on red plastic stools lined up in rows on the grass.
From beneath a sea of blue caps, supporters roared back in unison to call-and-response chants from candidate Lee Shu-chuan, a veteran technocrat and former deputy mayor of Taipei.
He was joined on stage by Taipei mayor Wayne Chiang Wan-an, who is running for a second term against DPP candidate Puma Shen Pao-yang. New Taipei City mayor Hou Yu-ih – who must step down after his second four-year term – was also at the rally, throwing his support behind Lee.
It was a different vibe across town that evening at a DPP campaign event where local musicians performed on a stage by the river. Supporters tied ribbons printed with campaign slogans to their backpacks, shopped for merch at stalls, and handed out badges.
After the show, DPP candidates including Su Chiao-hui – a lawmaker who is in the mayoral race against Lee – addressed the crowd.
Among the supporters at the KMT rally was Jennifer, a New Taipei City resident in her 30s who moved from mainland China and married a Taiwanese man about a decade ago. She said she wanted a stable life with her family and that she supported peaceful cross-strait reunification.
“I hope both sides can deepen exchanges, such as opening up tourism to boost the economy,” she said.
But her family did not know she was at the KMT rally – her in-laws are staunch DPP supporters.
Jennifer said she was not a fan of the DPP, mainly because of its adversarial stance towards Beijing and policies that affected some 369,000 mainland Chinese who – like her – are married to Taiwanese and moved to the island.
At the KMT rally (from third left) Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, New Taipei City mayor Hou Yu-ih, New Taipei City mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan, and Taoyuan mayor Chang San-cheng. Photo: Handout
She also doubted whether foreign powers such as the US or Japan would intervene to assist Taiwan in the event of a military conflict with Beijing.
“After Lai Ching-te took office, it has been all about constant confrontation with the mainland. He banks on protection from Japan and the United States,” she said. “But the friendly relations the US maintains with Taiwan on the surface are about selling weapons and securing high-end chips from Taiwan.”
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China, to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
Cross-strait relations deteriorated after the independence-leaning DPP came to power in 2016, and the situation has worsened since Lai became the island’s leader two years ago.
Another KMT supporter at the park was 40-year-old Stan, who said he would vote in Taipei for incumbent mayor Chiang, while his mother would back Lee in New Taipei City.
“I think the KMT is more likely to create opportunities for cross-strait peace and exchanges than the DPP. I hope there will be peace and better exchanges across the strait,” he said.
“I see more people travelling to mainland China. As tourists, they can witness the extent of development and progress in mainland China, which is more likely to influence how Taiwanese people perceive the mainland,” he added.
“I have been to [mainland] coastal cities like Shanghai and Xiamen, where the progress of urban development is very obvious. There is a lot for us to learn. Our way of living is very similar, although that of inland cities, like Kunming, could be quite different.”
Asked about his identity, Stan said “we are both Chinese”. “The division into two sides was a result of the civil war,” he said. “The differences in government systems are what people notice most, but culturally speaking we are the same.”
The DPP hold a rally across town in New Taipei City on Sunday. Photo: Handout
Across town at the DPP rally, security and cross-strait relations were the biggest concerns for 33-year-old Huang Cheng-ci.
“Being in a state of total hostility is certainly not a good thing. After all, nobody wants to get into a full-blown conflict or end up going to war,” he said.
As Beijing continued to pile pressure on Taiwan he said it was “very difficult to stand by indifferently”.
Huang said compulsory military service gave Taiwanese a direct way to connect with defence efforts, pointing to his own four-month stint in the military.
“If a conflict were to break out, having a segment of the male population with the military experience to respond is a favourable state of affairs,” he added.
On security partners like the US and Japan, Huang said international backing fundamentally depended on Taiwan’s own internal resolve.
“Whether others are willing to help is one thing, but we must first show our own determination and self-reliance to friendly countries,” he said.
Sandy Lue, a 56-year-old voter at the DPP rally, was more concerned about Beijing’s pressure campaign than an imminent military conflict.
“We are not worried about a war, but more about our own people slowly selling out Taiwan,” she said, referring to the Beijing-friendly KMT. “[Beijing] might also not favour a war, but take us back step by step.
New Taipei City mayoral candidate and lawmaker Su Chiao-hui (in white) at the DPP rally. Photo: Handout
“For people of my generation, speaking Taiwanese was forbidden back when we were in primary school. We experienced the restrictions imposed by the KMT and were shaped by that experience,” she said.
“However, my children – who are now in their 20s or 30s – never experienced that. They might think Taiwan has been developing well. The younger they are, the less they feel the threat.”
Lue said she hoped for stability. “I hope we maintain the status quo. Everyone wants to get on with their lives and make a living – they earn their money, we earn ours – and we can live together in peace,” she said, adding that trade could benefit businesses on both sides of the strait.
DPP mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (centre) addressed the crowd after local musicians performed. Photo: Handout
At the KMT rally, development and maintaining the status quo in cross-strait ties were front of mind for Michelle Ko, a 49-year-old mother of two teenage daughters.
“My family is quite neutral. We look at candidates one by one, rather than having a set stance of being Beijing-friendly,” said the New Taipei City resident.
“I would choose a party that leans towards maintaining the status quo,” she said. “With our children in mind, unforeseen changes seem very scary.”
By Holly Chik

title_en: Denmark bans headscarves for prosecutors as religious dress debate intensifies
content_en:
The new rules ensure that prosecutors, like judges, appear religiously and politically neutral when they take part in court hearings.
Protesters take part in a rally on the first day of the implementation of the face veil ban in Copenhagen on August 1, 2018. Photo: Ritzau Scanpix / Reuters
The Danish government issued new guidelines on Wednesday banning prosecutors from appearing in court while wearing religious headscarves.
The announcement came as the government debates whether to ban headscarves in schools and universities, and follows a 2018 ban on full-face Islamic veils such as the burka and niqab in public places.
“We are now introducing rules that require prosecutors, just as is the case for professional judges, to appear religiously and politically neutral when they take part in court hearings,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said in a statement.
“This includes religious headscarves, which prosecutors will no longer be allowed to wear in court.”
The minister did not state what consequences there would be for prosecutors who did not wish to remove their headscarves.
Women wearing niqab take part in a demonstration on August 1, 2018, the first day of the implementation of the Danish face veil ban. Photo: Ritzau Scanpix / AFP
Recently, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen expressed support for a ban on headscarves in primary and lower secondary schools – a proposal put forward by right-wing and far-right parties.
At the same time, Frederiksen voiced doubts about whether it could be implemented in a country where freedom of religion and freedom of expression are cardinal virtues.
Activists have long noted that headscarf bans amount to removing those freedoms from women by telling them what they can and cannot wear.
Frederiksen recently said that “in her eyes, the veil is an expression of oppression”.
The Social Democrat prime minister has been criticised for remarks she made last week about Denmark’s “great replacement”.
Her remarks were hailed by the Danish branch of the anti-immigration movement Generation Identity but Frederiksen said on Tuesday she refused to be equated with the far-right.
“I would like to make it clear that I do not wish to be lumped together with conspiracy theorists, far-right extremists or fascist movements. I have nothing good to say about any of them,” she wrote in a lengthy post on social media.
“There is nothing wrong with wanting to hold on to the country you love,” she argued.
Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen speaks to journalists in parliament on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters
Speaking on November 17 during a Danish political podcast with wide reach, Frederiksen said she was “not [a] supporter of a great replacement of the population”.
“We are a Danish society and our origin, our descent, is ethnically Danish,” she said.
“I am Danish and I am European, I believe in Danish and European values, and I do not want to compromise on them. The majority culture I want to see in Europe in the future is this one.”
A Norwegian survivor of the 2011 Utoya attacks in Norway took issue with Frederiksen’s remarks.
In July that year, neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik gunned down 77 people – most of them teenagers at a youth wing summer camp on the island of Utoya. Breivik, a fervent opponent of multiculturalism, committed the deadliest peacetime massacre in Norway’s history.
“I never would have believed I’d hear a European leader, let alone a social democrat, borrow the words from (the great replacement) theory,” Tarjei Jensen Bech wrote in Danish daily Politiken.
“I don’t believe you mean the same thing as Breivik,” he wrote. “The ‘great replacement of the population’ is not a neutral term. It has a history, and that history led to the deaths of young people on Utoya.”
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: As profits fall, China’s carmakers pass financial strain on to suppliers, expert says
content_en:
Automakers continue to face fierce competition, with some attempting to keep funds in reserve by extending payment cycles, squeezing suppliers.
An employee works on an electric vehicle production line in China’s eastern Jiangxi province. Photo: Xinhua
China’s auto industry faces mounting cash-flow pressure as receivables climb and collection periods lengthen amid a price war, an industry expert says, warning that the strain is squeezing suppliers’ finances and undermining long-term investment in innovation.
As of the end of September, outstanding receivables in China’s auto manufacturing sector had approached 3 trillion yuan (US$450 billion), their highest level in three years, Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association, wrote in a post on Tuesday.
Receivables, which represent money owed to companies by their customers, had risen steadily since February, Cui said, citing data from the National Bureau of Statistics.
“This shows that cash flow across the automotive supply chain is under severe strain,” Cui said, adding that carmakers, facing shrinking profit margins, were passing mounting financial pressure on to midstream component suppliers.
In the first three quarters, profits in the auto sector fell 23 per cent year on year, while its profit margin stood at just 3.3 per cent, compared with the 5.7 per cent average for industrial enterprises nationwide, according to Cui.
Meanwhile, the average receivables turnover period in the auto manufacturing sector has remained at about 100 days throughout this year, up from around 90 days last year.
As automakers continue to face pricing wars in a competitive industry, some are attempting to keep funds in reserve by delaying payment cycles to suppliers, Cui Dongshu says. Photo: Xinhua
As China’s carmakers continue to face fierce domestic competition, some have extended payment cycles to keep funds in reserve to offset industry-wide price drops.
However, Cui warned that the prolonged payment cycles were “draining smaller suppliers’ cash flow, putting them at risk of liquidity crises and leaving the industry with less capacity to invest in technological innovation”.
This could further fuel the vicious cycle of the price war, Cui added, warning that if smaller suppliers were driven out of business by financial pressures, carmakers would inevitably face supply disruptions and a decline in product quality.
Beijing has stepped up efforts to tackle the issue, releasing a dedicated notice in early September that requires carmakers to pay their parts suppliers and service providers within 60 days.
Regulators said they would also jointly summon companies with large outstanding payables, those deliberately extending payment terms and those facing repeated complaints from small and medium-sized suppliers.
“We need to ensure healthy cash flow throughout the supply chain and move away from a zero-sum game that hurts all parties,” Cui said in the post.
“Only then can China’s auto industry move beyond price competition towards higher-quality, mutually beneficial growth and compete more effectively in global markets.”

An employee works on an electric vehicle production line in China’s eastern Jiangxi province. Photo: Xinhua
China’s auto industry faces mounting cash-flow pressure as receivables climb and collection periods lengthen amid a price war, an industry expert says, warning that the strain is squeezing suppliers’ finances and undermining long-term investment in innovation.
As of the end of September, outstanding receivables in China’s auto manufacturing sector had approached 3 trillion yuan (US$450 billion), their highest level in three years, Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association, wrote in a post on Tuesday.
Receivables, which represent money owed to companies by their customers, had risen steadily since February, Cui said, citing data from the National Bureau of Statistics.
“This shows that cash flow across the automotive supply chain is under severe strain,” Cui said, adding that carmakers, facing shrinking profit margins, were passing mounting financial pressure on to midstream component suppliers.
In the first three quarters, profits in the auto sector fell 23 per cent year on year, while its profit margin stood at just 3.3 per cent, compared with the 5.7 per cent average for industrial enterprises nationwide, according to Cui.
Meanwhile, the average receivables turnover period in the auto manufacturing sector has remained at about 100 days throughout this year, up from around 90 days last year.
As automakers continue to face pricing wars in a competitive industry, some are attempting to keep funds in reserve by delaying payment cycles to suppliers, Cui Dongshu says. Photo: Xinhua
As China’s carmakers continue to face fierce domestic competition, some have extended payment cycles to keep funds in reserve to offset industry-wide price drops.
However, Cui warned that the prolonged payment cycles were “draining smaller suppliers’ cash flow, putting them at risk of liquidity crises and leaving the industry with less capacity to invest in technological innovation”.
This could further fuel the vicious cycle of the price war, Cui added, warning that if smaller suppliers were driven out of business by financial pressures, carmakers would inevitably face supply disruptions and a decline in product quality.
Beijing has stepped up efforts to tackle the issue, releasing a dedicated notice in early September that requires carmakers to pay their parts suppliers and service providers within 60 days.
Regulators said they would also jointly summon companies with large outstanding payables, those deliberately extending payment terms and those facing repeated complaints from small and medium-sized suppliers.
“We need to ensure healthy cash flow throughout the supply chain and move away from a zero-sum game that hurts all parties,” Cui said in the post.
“Only then can China’s auto industry move beyond price competition towards higher-quality, mutually beneficial growth and compete more effectively in global markets.”

title_en: Nepal hedges between ‘2 Asian giants’ as ties with India thaw
content_en:
Balendra Shah’s visit to New Delhi signals that Nepal is ready to reset ties with India despite their trade and territorial differences.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah wave a flag to remotely inaugurate a passenger train service between Ayodhya in India and Janakpur in Nepal after their meeting in New Delhi on Monday. Photo: AP
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s rapprochement with India highlights what analysts call the Himalayan nation’s delicate balancing act between two powerful neighbours, as Kathmandu eyes stronger ties with New Delhi without alienating Beijing.
During Shah’s two-day visit to India this week, when he met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, he secured a US$1.62 billion economic aid package from Delhi as Nepal struggles to recover from devastating floods in August.
It was Shah’s first visit to India after he became prime minister in late March following his Rastriya Swatantra Party’s victory in the March 5 general election.
The trip marked a departure from his reluctance to engage with Delhi after campaigning on a more independent Nepali foreign policy, according to analysts.
Shah’s visit from Sunday to Monday came after the floods killed 1,500 people and left 5,200 people missing. India sent rescue teams and relief materials to help Nepal recover from the disaster.
On Monday, India said it would provide Nepal with a US$1.62 billion economic package – one of its largest ever extended to any country – including a US$377 million grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects.
During the visit, both countries also signed agreements on energy cooperation and hydropower projects.
Houses in Dhunge, Nuwakot district, Nepal, damaged by the August 26 flash flood along the banks of the Trishuli River. Photo: AP
To boost tourism, Shah and Modi jointly flagged off the Saryu-Kamala express train on Monday, connecting Hindu pilgrimage sites in the Nepali city of Janakpur with the northern Indian city of Ayodhya.
Swaran Singh, an international relations analyst, said the bilateral meeting reflected India’s humanitarian help and “quiet diplomacy”.
“Shah recognises that keeping India at arm’s length can be economically costly. The rapprochement should endure, provided they can address sensitive issues like disputed territorial claims,” said Singh, a former professor of diplomacy and disarmament at Jawaharlal Nehru University.
While both countries enjoy long-standing economic and cultural ties, with hundreds of thousands of Nepalis living and working in India, they have disputed over their common borders and trade.
Nepal has objected to India’s use of the Lipulekh Pass, a Himalayan mountain pass in a district of the Indian state of Uttarakhand, for a pilgrimage route.
Compulsory laboratory testing on all imported tea consignments imposed by India’s Tea Board in May effectively halted tea shipments from Nepal for about two months, forcing Nepali factories to shut down before Delhi allowed exports to resume in late June.
Over the past decade, China has expanded trade with Nepal, exporting more electronic products and electric vehicles, and has developed its sectors, including infrastructure such as the Pokhara International Airport, health and education.
Among the key projects in the pipeline is the China-Nepal Friendship Industrial Park, backed by Chinese investment under the Belt and Road Initiative.
Passengers wait outside the Pokhara International Airport in Nepal. Photo: China News Service/Getty Images
“Shah’s visit marks a consequential diplomatic recalibration, but it will be a bit too ambitious to call it a complete reset or diplomatic breakthrough. There still exist serious structural differences,” Singh said.
Nonetheless, the visit signalled the importance of the two countries’ cultural and economic ties anchored by their shared history and geography, Singh added.
Nepal’s government has estimated the flood damage at US$5 billion. The World Bank has assessed the physical damage to be US$1.7 billion, with Nepal requiring US$4.8 billion to fund its recovery and reconstruction.
In a report on November 12, Fitch Ratings projected Nepal’s GDP to fall to 3.4 per cent in the financial year ending mid-July 2027, from 3.9 per cent in the previous financial year. The floods, which affected more than 10 per cent of the country’s power capacity and hit tourism and transport, would weigh on its near-term growth, Fitch said.
Uday Chandra, a professor at India’s Ashoka University, said Shah came to power after promising a break with Nepal’s political establishment, including its traditional dependence on India.
Chandra noted that about 80 per cent of Nepal’s external trade involved India, whether as direct exports or reshipment.
The visit reflected Shah’s “acknowledgement of the unavoidable economic and geographical realities that bind the two countries together”, with the economic aid package as well as plans for closer energy and transport connectivity emerging as “the fruits of rapprochement”, he added.
Shah’s visit signalled that Nepal would remain “a hedge between two Asian giants”, with the country needing India and China for its continuous development, Chandra said.
Then Bangladesh’s prime minister Sheikh Hasina speaking to the media in Dhaka in January 2024 after she won the country’s parliamentary elections. Photo: AFP
The visit happened against the backdrop of India’s continuously strained relations with Bangladesh, where an uprising led to the downfall of then prime minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024 and a new government took office in February after a general election.
The two countries have disagreed over issues including Dhaka’s call for the extradition of Hasina from India and the 1996 Ganga water-sharing treaty, which is set to expire on December 12.
Priyajit Debsarkar, a London-based geopolitical analyst specialising in South Asia, noted that Bangladesh needed to boost cooperation with India to address its economic challenges, including its energy crisis.
In August, Delhi confirmed that Bangladesh had requested India’s help to supply extra fuel.
Chandra said that the new governments in Nepal and Bangladesh were aiming for “rapprochement on pragmatic grounds” towards India.
Nonetheless, this had to be balanced with what voters in the two countries wanted over ties with India, he added.
“Political transitions in Nepal and Bangladesh have brought to power leaders with their own domestic middle-class constituencies, national priorities, and expectations of greater autonomy from New Delhi.”
By Biman Mukherji

title_en: ‘I don’t know what world will be like’ when AI understands physics, Edward Witten says
content_en:
Fields medallist tells how AI could be a turning point for modern physics as it shows ‘superhuman powers in mathematics’.
American physicist Edward Witten, who has cited AI as an assistant in his recent research, says he is not hesitant about integrating AI into his research workflow. Photo: Getty Images
Recent AI breakthroughs in solving mathematical problems could mark a turning point in understanding modern physics, according to one of the world’s top physicists.
American Edward Witten, an emeritus professor at the Institute for Advanced Study (IAS), is a leading figure in the fields of theoretical and mathematical physics.
In 1990, Witten became the first physicist to be awarded the Fields Medal – widely regarded as the highest honour in mathematics – for applying ideas from theoretical physics to solve major mathematical problems.
[embedded media]
Witten, who has cited AI as an assistant in his recent research, said he was not hesitant about integrating AI into his research workflow.
“But I do not know what the world will be like when AI really understands physics well,” he said on November 18.
“That is something that mathematicians are grappling with now, because AI has developed in some ways superhuman powers in mathematics.”
In October, OpenAI released hundreds of preprints covering mathematical problems generated by its models. Earlier this month, a mathematician at Anthropic said he and AI assistance Claude had solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis.
Witten, who has spent some time looking at the OpenAI proofs, said the proof of a fundamental statement about the quantum Yang-Mills theory “could be a turning point in mathematical understanding of modern physics”. The theory, introduced in the early 1950s by physicists Chen-ning Yang and Robert Mills, is a foundational framework for the Standard Model of particle physics.
While visiting Hong Kong for a lecture this month, Witten became a trending topic on Chinese social media after a photo circulated showing his computer projecting a Claude pop-up that said the AI assistant was not available in the region.
Anthropic, Claude’s creator, blocks access to the large language model in mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau. In papers published this year, Witten has credited Claude as an assistant in his research.
Witten is a member of an independent advisory group hosted at IAS that helps advise OpenAI and any other companies on the communication of their results in line with academic mathematics standards.
While mathematicians are already having to grapple with how to interact with AI and channel it to advance their research, Witten said physicists were a couple of years behind because it was harder for AI to understand physics.
“But I am not making predictions about the future. It caught up in math incredibly fast. And who knows what it will do in physics in a couple years,” he said.
“I look forward to being able to discuss physics with a machine that is interested in physics and able to discuss it.”
Edward Witten (above) became a trending topic on Chinese social media after his computer was shown to project a Claude pop-up (below) that said the AI assistant was not available in the region. Photo: Handout
Photo: Handout
Witten earned an undergraduate degree in history before receiving a doctorate in physics at Princeton University in 1976. He was a professor at the university from 1980 to 1987.
In 1987, he became a faculty member at IAS – which has been home to researchers such as Albert Einstein and Robert Oppenheimer – where he became an emeritus professor in 2022.
He has won several prestigious awards for his work in both maths and physics, including the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics in 2012.
Following a proposal in 1995, Witten helped unify various versions of string theory into a single framework called M-theory.
String theory is a theoretical framework that proposes that the universe’s fundamental building blocks are tiny vibrating strings rather than point-like particles. Much like notes on a violin, the specific ways these strings vibrate determine the type of particles we observe.
The theory has led to scepticism, as it lacks direct experimental confirmation and the conditions needed to test it remain out of reach.
Witten, who is revisiting work he did decades ago in open string field theory, said it was understandable that some physicists were sceptical, as the “reasons for thinking that string theory is important are largely circumstantial”.
“There’s not a bulletproof argument that it’s definitely part of the way to describe the natural world,” he added.
Witten’s lecture in Hong Kong was on black hole thermodynamics, a field that he said teaches us something “amazing and bizarre” about the relationship between gravity and quantum mechanics – the two main theories that form the basis of modern physics.
While Einstein’s theory of gravity – based on curved space-time – is important for planets, stars and the universe, quantum mechanics is important for microscopic things, like atoms, molecules and subatomic particles.
However, contradictions emerge when these two theories are combined. According to Witten, there are two areas where useful insights have been seen beyond this contradiction.
The first is string theory, where he said the contradiction was apparently avoided, but noted that we do not really understand the theory. The second is black hole thermodynamics, where curved space-time is related to thermodynamics.
“One thing everyone knows about a black hole is that what falls in doesn’t come out. It’s a one-way trip. So falling into a black hole is irreversible,” Witten said.
However, in physics, it is believed to be impossible for a black body to only absorb and not emit. In 1974, Stephen Hawking discovered that quantum-mechanically, black holes do emit radiation at a very low temperature.
“Falling into a black hole is like breaking an egg. In practice, it can’t be reversed,” Witten said.
“But if you were incredibly powerful and could precisely set the right initial conditions, then you could put the egg back together again and get somebody to come out of the black hole.”
While Einstein’s theory describes black holes classically, Witten said there was more to the story quantum-mechanically, which is why physicists investigated black hole thermodynamics.
Owing to new techniques emerging over the past decade, “observationally, black holes are much more alive than they were in the past”, he said.
Witten, who was a speaker at the Riemann Bicentennial Conference held in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen this month, said it was “very important for science to be borderless”.
“It’s terrible that in many fields, collaboration with China is so difficult now,” he said.
Witten noted that while in purely theoretical areas there were fewer obstacles to the exchange of ideas, there remained barriers to the movement of people, such as obtaining visas.
[embedded media]
On US-China collaboration, Witten said it was a “shame that the world, in some ways, has moved in the wrong direction in that regard”.
In an article he wrote with American theoretical physicist David Gross in 2015, the two said a proposed “Great Collider” in China had the potential to transform particle physics.
The ambitious plan for the Circular Electron Positron Collider, led by physicist Wang Yifang, hit a roadblock last year when it was not put forth for consideration in China’s latest five-year plan. Wang said his team planned to submit the proposal again in 2030 unless CERN’s similar project received official approval before then.
“It would be great if China would revive that in the next five-year plan,” Witten said.
He pointed to a similar proposal at CERN that did not yet have an ironclad commitment from countries, noting that China could also join that project if it went ahead.
By Victoria Bela

title_en: China promises to help Thailand and Myanmar fight Mekong basin pollution
content_en:
Parts of Thailand are at risk of water shortages as a result of arsenic poisoning that has been blamed on unregulated mining in Shan State.
Upstream mining has polluted some rivers in the Mekong basin.  Photo: Handout
China pledged on Wednesday to work with Thailand and Myanmar to tackle river pollution along the border between the two Southeast Asian nations.
Residents in northern Thailand are facing potential water shortages and supply disruptions due to unregulated gold and rare earth mining upstream in northeastern Myanmar that has severely contaminated some tributaries of the Mekong with unsafe levels of arsenic.
Bangkok asked Beijing to help close down the mines during talks between the three countries to discuss the crisis on Tuesday.
It also asked for help in identifying the mines and tracing the minerals produced there.
Thai officials said all three countries had agreed that mining operations in Shan State were the source of the contamination of Thailand’s Kok and Sai rivers.
Beijing also acknowledged during the meeting that private Chinese companies operated some mines in the area and that some of the resources extracted were shipped to China, they added.
China did not issue an official statement following the meeting.
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the country would dispatch specialists and provide technical support to a joint Thailand-Myanmar working group investigating the problem.
However, he stopped short of explicitly endorsing Thailand’s call to halt the mining for at least six months, instead urging the authorities to “identify the root causes” through “science-based, professional and objective” investigations before drawing conclusions.
“We stand ready to work with Thailand and Myanmar to enhance cooperation on water resources governance, share experience, strengthen capacity and jointly protect the environment of the Mekong River basin,” Guo said.
Guo said Beijing required Chinese enterprises overseas to comply with their host countries’ laws and regulations and opposed activities that harmed the environment.
[embedded media]
The pollution has been linked to a surge in mining activity in Myanmar following the 2021 coup and the subsequent conflict and economic collapse that left the industry largely unregulated.
Last weekend, Bangkok announced plans to tighten controls on mineral imports and exports passing through Thailand from Myanmar.
The measures were designed to close legal loopholes and prevent Thailand from serving as a conduit for Myanmar’s uncontrolled mining operations, according to local media.
Thailand has also committed to identifying the source of the contamination by analysing the arsenic’s unique characteristics.
Thai Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said the government was collaborating with a Chinese scientific institute and Mae Fah Luang University in Chiang Rai to establish an advanced testing laboratory based on Chinese standards.

China pledged on Wednesday to work with Thailand and Myanmar to tackle river pollution along the border between the two Southeast Asian nations.
Residents in northern Thailand are facing potential water shortages and supply disruptions due to unregulated gold and rare earth mining upstream in northeastern Myanmar that has severely contaminated some tributaries of the Mekong with unsafe levels of arsenic.
Bangkok asked Beijing to help close down the mines during talks between the three countries to discuss the crisis on Tuesday.
It also asked for help in identifying the mines and tracing the minerals produced there.
Thai officials said all three countries had agreed that mining operations in Shan State were the source of the contamination of Thailand’s Kok and Sai rivers.
Beijing also acknowledged during the meeting that private Chinese companies operated some mines in the area and that some of the resources extracted were shipped to China, they added.
China did not issue an official statement following the meeting.
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the country would dispatch specialists and provide technical support to a joint Thailand-Myanmar working group investigating the problem.
However, he stopped short of explicitly endorsing Thailand’s call to halt the mining for at least six months, instead urging the authorities to “identify the root causes” through “science-based, professional and objective” investigations before drawing conclusions.
“We stand ready to work with Thailand and Myanmar to enhance cooperation on water resources governance, share experience, strengthen capacity and jointly protect the environment of the Mekong River basin,” Guo said.
Guo said Beijing required Chinese enterprises overseas to comply with their host countries’ laws and regulations and opposed activities that harmed the environment.
[embedded media]
The pollution has been linked to a surge in mining activity in Myanmar following the 2021 coup and the subsequent conflict and economic collapse that left the industry largely unregulated.
Last weekend, Bangkok announced plans to tighten controls on mineral imports and exports passing through Thailand from Myanmar.
The measures were designed to close legal loopholes and prevent Thailand from serving as a conduit for Myanmar’s uncontrolled mining operations, according to local media.
Thailand has also committed to identifying the source of the contamination by analysing the arsenic’s unique characteristics.
Thai Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said the government was collaborating with a Chinese scientific institute and Mae Fah Luang University in Chiang Rai to establish an advanced testing laboratory based on Chinese standards.

title_en: Huawei forms patent teams for chips and AI, eyeing ecosystem to rival Nvidia
content_en:
With AI and chips now generating more inventions than telecoms, IP chief says effort aims to attract developers, partners and customers.
People view Huawei’s Atlas 950 SuperPoD computing system for data centres at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 17. Photo: AFP
Huawei Technologies has established dedicated patent teams for semiconductors and artificial intelligence as it seeks to establish an overseas foothold for a computing ecosystem to rival Nvidia’s.
Extending an intellectual property (IP) operation rooted in telecommunications, the Shenzhen-based company had now created a semiconductor IP team and an AI-focused unit, with some engineers transferred from research and development departments, chief IP officer Alan Fan told South China Morning Post on Tuesday.
The effort supports Huawei’s push to take its latest large-scale computing systems overseas. At the MWC Barcelona tech show in March, the company introduced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, built around its Ascend AI processors, and the TaiShan 950 SuperPoD, based on general-purpose processors.
The overseas push extends Huawei’s challenge to Nvidia in a contest to lure international developers, hardware partners and customers. Nvidia’s Cuda platform supplies programming tools and software libraries that developers use to build applications for its chips. Huawei is promoting its own Cann software platform alongside Ascend.
Fan said Huawei wanted to work with companies in Europe and Japan whose technologies complemented its own, as it sought to build an international ecosystem around its products.
“Of course we hope these standards will be international and these partnerships will be cross-border,” he said.
Wireless communications accounted for 41 per cent of Huawei’s active granted patents at the end of 2025. AI and computing accounted for 13 per cent, making it the third-largest category, according to Huawei.
Fan said Huawei was now generating more innovations in computing and AI infrastructure, prompting the company to put more resources into protecting them.
The main purpose is to protect our ecosystem and the features that make our products competitiveAlan Fan, chief IP officer, Huawei
“Our own investment is indeed increasing,” he said. “There are so many inventions being produced that are worth protecting.”
For the computing business, patents help protect Huawei’s distinctive technologies while allowing partners to build complementary products, Fan said. The company can recover its investment through sales of chips and systems.
“The main purpose is to protect our ecosystem and the features that make our products competitive,” he said.
Huawei was offering free licensing of patents covering UnifiedBus, its technology for connecting processors, to encourage other chipmakers to develop components that work with its systems, Fan said.
Opening the specifications could attract companies making peripheral chips, boards and connectors. Fan said Huawei was not always able to make simpler components cost-effectively, giving it a reason to bring other suppliers into the ecosystem.
He described Huawei’s approach to connecting chips as “more open” than Nvidia’s. The US company has also expanded access to its interconnect technology through partnerships with other chip designers.
In September, rotating chairman Eric Xu said Huawei was supplying limited volumes of AI chips to some countries, but domestic demand was limiting its capacity for a broader international expansion.
Huawei reported around US$800 million in patent licensing revenue in 2025, up 27 per cent from US$630 million a year earlier.
Fan said the IP department was not run as a profit centre. Its work ultimately supported Huawei’s operating businesses by helping to attract developers and sell more products and services, he said.
By Howard Liu
