title_en: Jensen Huang is back. The risk to Nvidia and the AI boom remains
content_en:
A massively profitable industry spent two weeks unsure whether its biggest supplier could still raise money, book factory time and buy memory chips.
US President Donald Trump (right) stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science during a summit at the US Institute of Peace in Washington on October 8. Photo: Reuters
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12, yet on November 23 the board reinstated him. In the intervening days, the company lost around a trillion dollars in market value. When the news of Huang’s reinstatement broke on Monday, Nvidia shares jumped more than 30 per cent and recovered nearly all the losses that followed his exit. Staff crowded the Nvidia headquarters lobby in Santa Clara, California, to welcome him back.
The trouble began on October 29, when The New York Times reported that Washington officials believed a business executive close to Huang worked for Chinese intelligence. On November 8, Huang admitted to his staff that he’d had an extramarital affair. Further reports spoke of relationships with multiple colleagues. Only a few days before Huang’s return, the Nvidia board of directors said it was not considering reinstating him.
Then the mood changed quickly. The board said it had spoken with senior US officials and was sure Huang’s return posed no risk to national security. US President Donald Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board, both directly and indirectly. Lawmakers from both major US parties objected to the move, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta said an inquiry into Nvidia’s China dealings would continue.
I see a board that had to choose between a market in free fall and a White House that wanted its champion back. A company this large will always feel the weight of politics. Still, directors who reverse their decisions in just 11 days amid a presidential push will have trouble claiming they run an independent firm.
Nvidia has no named successor and no chief operating officer. Dozens of senior managers report directly to Huang. When he left, nobody could say who would make the hard calls, and the market priced in chaos. His return temporarily ends that chaos, but the move matters well beyond the share price of one company.
Nvidia has built a financing platform of up to US$500 billion with big investment firms to help pay for data centres. Bank of America estimates it also held about US$70 billion in stakes in artificial intelligence (AI) firms as of August, including new cloud rental companies. Analysts feared those deals could slow or cost more without their chief deal maker. Research firm SemiAnalysis said Huang’s personal ties helped win chipmaking capacity in Taiwan and memory supply in Korea. Those ties remain in place.
[embedded media]
The week showed how thin the base of the AI boom is. A massively profitable industry spent two weeks unsure whether its biggest supplier could still raise money, book factory time and buy memory chips. All of that rested on one person’s reputation and contacts list.
That is a fragile way to build the base of a new technology. Nvidia extends credit to customers, and those customers then buy Nvidia chips. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk warns that the sector could run short of cash and that many of the 200 or so small neocloud firms will fail, while Huang says demand will carry them. If the Nvidia leader is wrong, the same single point of trust will be under scrutiny again.
Big buyers are watching, too. Google, Amazon and Microsoft already design their own chips. Any customer who saw their supply hinge on the fortunes of one man will want a second source. Expect the shift to custom chips to accelerate, even as Nvidia keeps its lead.
A person stands in front of an electronic board displaying rising stock prices at the Taiwan Stock Exchange in Taipei on November 24 as markets reacted to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s return to the company. Photo: Reuters
Export policy is the next test. After the scandal broke, Washington did as many expected and tightened limits on advanced chips reaching China, especially through middlemen. Congress is already talking about new chip security laws. Huang has said that cutting off China is unrealistic and that curbs on chip exports do little. He returns under a security cloud, so he will have little room to say it again.
There is a wider lesson here. The people who run AI firms hold secrets that governments want. Their travel, meetings and private lives are all targets for foreign intelligence. Boards used to treat that as a matter for the legal team. They should now treat it as a board duty. Boards should require clear rules on contact with foreign business partners and honest reports when a rule is violated.
Taiwan’s supply chain barely changed during Huang’s absence. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, Foxconn and Quanta still face strong demand. Huang was born in Taiwan and spent years building trust with Taiwanese firms. Nvidia’s board should ask that this trust be written into contracts, teams and routines. A good relationship should survive the person who started it.
[embedded media]
Meanwhile, Huang must deliver on his pledge to Nvidia staff that he will do better the second time round. The easy promise involves himself and his personal life. The harder one involves his company.
Huang should publicly name a successor and hire a chief operating officer. The board should require regular reports from him. Congress and the White House will be watching. Nvidia’s financing platform should stand on assets and contracts, not on one man’s credit.
If he does these things, Nvidia will be stronger than it was before the fall. If he does not, history will repeat itself. When the next crisis happens, the market will teach everyone a much harder lesson.
By Chang Ruay-Shiung

title_en: Gen Z’s digital activism stops short of sustained civic action
content_en:
Readers discuss the challenge of turning political awareness into constructive advocacy, and Pakistan’s growing diplomatic influence.
An elderly man in Wan Chai, Hong Kong. In this city of remarkable global reach, pressing local issues such as elderly poverty and waste management still struggle to command sustained civic advocacy. Photo: Nora Tam
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words.
Not long ago, I came across a string of social media videos in which frustrated New York residents filmed neighbourhood potholes and called on their mayor, Zohran Mamdani, to “fix” them. These clips shared the assumption that if a problem is broadcast loudly enough online, someone in authority will step in to fix it. Those clips stayed with me, as they seemed to capture a defining paradox in Gen Z’s relationship with public life.
We live in what is easily the most politically aware era in human history, an age where a teenager in Hong Kong can follow debates in Washington or distant conflicts in real time from a phone in their pocket. Yet while digital activism and street protests have surged around the world (“By all memes: why Asia’s Gen Z are revolting”, November 14), this visibility masks a quieter shortfall: our constructive involvement in policymaking, sustained civic advocacy and everyday community volunteering remains remarkably low.
Across the globe, young people express genuine concern over social issues as they step back from the slow, unglamorous work of institutional life, leaving youth voter turnout lagging and online outrage rarely maturing into workable policy. If we are truly the most informed generation in history, it is worth asking why our hands-on civic contribution is moving in the opposite direction.
Cynicism offers one explanation, since coming of age amid financial crises, soaring housing costs and climate anxiety makes disengagement feel less like apathy and more like a weary resignation. Still, those very pressures should provoke the opposite instinct, leaving me to wonder why those of us with the greatest stake in future policy remain content to watch from the sidelines.
This tension feels especially familiar in Hong Kong, a city of remarkable global reach where pressing local issues – elderly poverty, waste management, ethnic minority inclusion and the welfare of migrant domestic workers – still struggle to command sustained civic advocacy.
Ultimately, our generation has to recognise that the real challenge before us is turning unprecedented awareness into a renewed sense of agency – one that actually drives civic advocacy and institutional participation – or else we risk becoming history’s most informed spectators, and spectators rarely change the course of events.
Samyuktha Parameswaran, research and content associate, Global Institute for Tomorrow
Pakistan a vital diplomatic bridge in Gulf security
Two recent opinion articles in the South China Morning Post identify limits in Middle East diplomacy. In “As US-Iran war shows, China’s influence can’t secure its line to Gulf oil” (November 4), the writer notes that Beijing’s commercial and diplomatic clout has not protected energy access routes. Similarly, in “The big test facing the Middle East’s emerging security autonomy” (November 18), the writer asks whether overlapping relationships can become arrangements that restrain force and protect commerce. Both leave out a state where those questions meet: Pakistan.
Pakistan is close to Beijing, borders Iran and carries security credibility in Gulf capitals. It signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia in 2025, joined Riyadh and Ankara in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, and signed the Badr memorandum of understanding on defence-industrial cooperation with Turkey, Qatar and Indonesia in October. It also hosted the April US-Iran talks, the highest-level direct contact between the two countries since 1979, signed the June Islamabad memorandum as mediator, and has recently heard Iran’s foreign minister say Tehran trusts its mediation.
That combination is no accident. Pakistan’s energy costs and Gulf remittances are exposed to every escalation, so it has a direct stake in preventing a wider war.
Its diplomacy is also widening. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Egypt coordinate as the “regional four”, formed in Riyadh in March. On October 23, their foreign ministers met counterparts from Britain, France, Germany and Italy in Istanbul, and days later, security chiefs from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran. No single outside power can easily replicate that web of channels.
Security pacts will restrain escalation only if they are paired with practical diplomatic off-ramps. The Mecca partners describe their pact as collective deterrence, and that framing will be credible only if matched by diplomacy that engages Tehran’s stated conditions, including sanctions relief, frozen assets and an end to the US naval blockade.
Frameworks to protect shipping and reduce tension should not treat regional states as bystanders. They should draw on actors, Pakistan among them, that keep channels open to every side. Beijing, whose Gulf strategy this war has tested, has good reason to back such efforts.
Zainab Malaika, Islamabad, Pakistan

title_en: US-China trade war stuck in limbo as Trump nears new tariffs
content_en:
China and 15 other US trade partners may soon face new overcapacity levies as the Trump administration rebuilds tariff walls.
US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping take part in bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. Photo: AFP
The United States is reportedly readying new tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners following a months-long inquiry into state support and excess industrial capacity.
Results from the US Trade Representative (USTR) investigation may be announced as soon as this week, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the plans. The inquiry looked at whether subsidies and other measures had created overcapacity overseas, leading to a global flood of low-cost exports that hurt US companies.
Findings from the report may give the Trump administration a new legal rationale for imposing levies as it works to rebuild tariff walls struck down by the US Supreme Court in February. Any new taxes would be in addition to the 10-12.5 per cent levies imposed in July to penalise countries for failing to block goods produced using forced labour.
The size of the new levies is not yet clear, the Journal said. Still, they will reflect trade deals signed before the Supreme Court ruling, the people said. That suggests rates of no more than 15 per cent for the European Union, Japan and South Korea. Rates for Vietnam and India could be higher.
China will probably be hit with a higher tariff, as Trump officials see its industrial subsidies as particularly extensive and disruptive, the Journal said. The US Trade Representative declined to comment and The White House didn’t respond to inquiries, the newspaper said.
Most exports will be hit by the new levies, aside from some industrial goods, such as steel, aluminium and vehicles, which are already subject to separate national-security tariffs, the report said. Language in the tariff order may also allow for further increases if overcapacity is not addressed, some of the people said.
China faces increasing global complaints about overcapacity as surging exports put its trade surplus on track to beat last year’s record US$1.2 trillion. The EU, for instance, is working on a number of trade defences as European companies shed workers amid a flood of low-cost Chinese imports.
[embedded media]
Related news:
US planemaker Boeing booked its first major mainland China deal since 2017 after Xiamen Airlines ordered 50 737 Max 8 aircraft. The carrier, a unit of China Southern Airlines, got a discount on the US$7.4 billion list price for the jets, according to a company statement. The planes will be delivered from 2031 to 2034. China indicated plans to buy 200 Boeing aircraft in May during US President Donald Trump’s state visit to Beijing. How others reported it

In contrast, Trump administration officials do not pretend that their president’s word is his bond. Unblushingly, they portray his unreliability as a sign of strength and cleverness. In this, Trump-era America resembles Russia and Iran more than it does a traditional great power. (The Economist)

The SCMP Plus takeaway

President Donald Trump seems set to renew his love of tariffs, while probably keeping China levies much lower than the 34 per cent rate announced on “Liberation Day” last year. He has repeatedly boasted of good relations with President Xi Jinping, even as members of the US Congress push for a much tougher line.
China has shown more bark than bite lately in US trade relations. It has complained about new controls on high-end AI chips without making any retaliatory moves. The country has also ordered some new Boeing aircraft – if fewer than Trump might have hoped – and temporarily prolonged a pause on critical-mineral export controls.
Whether the shaky status quo can be turned into something more permanent may become clear in December when Trump and Xi Jinping are likely to meet in Miami alongside a G20 summit. China is unlikely to want to upset the apple cart now when exports are propping up weak economic growth. Similarly, Trump’s enthusiasm for tariffs may be tempered by the fact that higher prices contributed to the Republicans’ midterm trouncing. Stock markets, which are fragile, to say the least, are a further deterrent to starting a trade fight.
Still, there’s no guarantee that the US will hold China tariffs below the 20 per cent ceiling. The USTR is yet to announce the new duties, and the door could be open for higher punitive fees. Bessent and Greer complained to He earlier this month about China’s failures to live up to commitments on agricultural purchases and rare-earth exports.
Trump could see tariffs as a useful distraction from the furore over his role in Jensen Huang’s return to US chip giant Nvidia after a spy scandal. They could also help to deflect criticism about the administration being too lax in letting Chinese companies circumvent export controls on high-end chips.
Either way, it’s unlikely that the tariffs will be implemented before the December summit, so they could end up being just another bargaining chip.
Until then, expect more half-pulled punches rather than any major threats to the two countries’ “constructive relationship of strategic stability”.

title_en: Beijing weighs mergers, stricter rules to revitalise struggling airlines: sources
content_en:
The plan aims to accelerate the years-long effort to improve profitability, sources said, which may also affect airline procurement decisions.
A Chongqing Airlines Airbus jet seen at Singapore’s Changi Airport on September 21, 2025. Photo: Shutterstock Images
China’s civil aviation regulator is studying options for a sweeping consolidation of the sector starting next year, including mergers and restructuring options for smaller, loss-making carriers, according to industry insiders.
The plan, still being sketched out, aimed to accelerate a years-long effort to improve profitability, which could also affect airline procurement decisions, including their demand for new jets from Boeing and Airbus, the sources said.
“The overall number of domestic airlines in the next few years … by 2030, may drop as a result [of such mergers],” said one source with a major state-owned carrier, citing the plan being considered by the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC).
It remained unclear, however, whether the CAAC would cap the number of airlines, the source added, declining to be named as they were not authorised to speak to media.
The source also said the CAAC could further raise capital formation thresholds and other requirements for new entrants and implement a more clearly defined mechanism for exiting the industry.
Requirements being considered included higher registered capital for passenger airlines and official guidelines for and supervision of mergers, reorganisations as well as dissolution and liquidation, the sources said.
The planned changes come after the CAAC issued a document in August that clarified its authority to mandate that carriers “rectify irregularities” or face possible suspension of operations or revocation of their licenses.
The regulatory focus next year would be on airlines with “persistent safety hazards, low operational efficiency and high financial risks”, according to the source.
The Boeing logo seen on its factory in Renton, Washington state, US, April 15, 2026. Photo: Reuters
The effort is still in the early stages and the details, including any merger targets, process and timeline, were not yet finalised, according to sources.
Some small but heavily indebted operators once backed by their respective local governments and bearing the names of cities could be merged, said a second source.
“If they fail to identify a buyer or secure adequate funding from major shareholders, some of them may eventually go out of business, just like how Spirit Airlines in the US collapsed,” the second source said.
More mergers would also impact plane manufacturers. If the big three Chinese carriers absorbed smaller rivals, they could need to reassess their procurement plans with Boeing and Airbus, according to the second source.
“Since this year, the big three have signed significant deals with Airbus, but now, some optional orders or purchase pledges may be slower to materialise or even be withdrawn,” the source said.
Airbus has projected that China will need 8,830 new passenger aircraft over the next 20 years, about 20 per cent of the global total.
However, the industry as a whole is still struggling to achieve pre-Covid profitability.
Last year, industry-wide profits, including those for airlines and airport operators, reached 6.5 billion yuan (US$975 million), with the industry only turning a profit a year earlier for the first time since 2020, according to official data. In 2019, total industry profits were 54.1 billion yuan.
An Airbus A330-343 aircraft operated by China Eastern Airlines is directed to the runway at Beijing Capital International Airport on August 10, 2024. Photo: Shutterstock Images
China Southern posted a net loss of 4.3 billion yuan, China Eastern lost 2.1 billion yuan and Air China lost 2 billion yuan, according to company reports.
Competition from high-speed rail services and soaring fuel prices amid the Middle East conflict have eroded earnings for the operators.
Smaller operators face even greater challenges to keep flying.
In May, Chongqing withdrew from a 4.5 billion yuan cash injection in Chongqing Airlines, a joint venture between China Southern and the city government. Urumqi Air and Fuzhou Airlines also have inadequate assets to cover debts, according to their financial disclosures and mainland media reports.
Last year, reports went viral about pilots from Xian-based Joy Air switching jobs to work as food delivery workers after the carrier suspended operations.
As such, mergers could help a recovery in profitability, according to a report published in October by Beijing-based travel consultancy TravelZone.
“By 2030, the number of domestic airlines may drop from the current 65 to 55 or 60 via mergers,” the report said.
“With fewer airlines, it is hoped that the growth of seats and fleet capacity can be suppressed below demand growth [to enable] a systemic recovery between 2027–2030,” TravelZone said.
By Frank Chen
